title: Tamang Culture and Homestays in Langtang
meta_description: Tamang culture in Langtang: who the Tamang are, Buddhism and jhankri traditions, Tamang Selo music, Sonam Lhosar, and homestays in Gatlang, Briddim and Thuman.
summary: Most villages in the Langtang region are Tamang, one of Nepal's largest ethnic groups, with Tibetan-influenced Buddhism, shamanic traditions, Tamang Selo music and stone-built villages. The best way to experience their culture is a homestay in Gatlang, Briddim or Thuman on the Tamang Heritage Trail, or Hyolmo homes in Helambu.

sections.heading: Who the Tamang are
paras: The Tamang are one of Nepal's largest ethnic groups, living mainly in the hills around the Kathmandu Valley, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Sindhupalchok and Makwanpur districts. In the Langtang region, they make up most of the population of Syabrubesi, Dhunche, Langtang village, Thulo Syabru, Gatlang, Thuman and Briddim. They speak Tamang, a Tibeto-Burman language, at home and Nepali in public life, and many families have relatives in Kathmandu, especially around Boudhanath.

Historically, Tamang communities farmed steep terraces of millet, maize, barley and potatoes and kept cattle, sheep and yaks, trading salt and goods along routes to Tibet through Kerung. Many men also worked as porters, and today trekking and tourism are major sources of income in the Langtang Valley. The 2015 earthquake hit Tamang areas especially hard, destroying homes in Langtang, Gatlang and many other villages, and much of what visitors see has been rebuilt since.

sections.heading: Religion: lamas, gompas and jhankri
paras: Tamang religious life combines Tibetan Buddhism with older shamanic traditions. Most villages have a gompa, or monastery, where lamas lead prayers, funerals and festivals, and chortens, mani walls and prayer flags mark the trails. Water-driven prayer wheels in the upper Langtang Valley turn day and night. Visitors should walk clockwise around religious structures, keeping them on their right.

Alongside the lamas are the bombo or jhankri, shamans who heal, protect against spirits and communicate with local deities through drumming, chanting and trance. The most visible gathering of jhankri is at Gosaikunda on Janai Purnima, when shamans in white robes and feathered headdresses dance around the lake through the full-moon night. Many Tamang also observe Hindu festivals such as Dashain, reflecting centuries of shared life in Nepal's hills.

sections.heading: Music, dress and festivals
paras: Tamang Selo is the community's best-known folk music: call-and-response songs about love, work and village life, sung to the beat of the damphu, a round frame drum. Evenings in Gatlang or Briddim often end with Selo singing and dancing around the fire, and community groups perform for visitors. Traditional dress is still worn by many women, especially older women and on festival days, with wrapped skirts, aprons, heavy jewellery and headscarves.

The biggest celebration is Sonam Lhosar, the Tamang New Year, in January or February, marked by cleaning and decorating homes, new prayer flags, gompa visits, family feasts and Selo dancing. Buddha Jayanti in spring and Dashain in autumn are also widely celebrated. In August, many Tamang join pilgrims at Gosaikunda and visit Parvati Kunda above Gatlang.

sections.heading: Where to stay with Tamang families
paras: The Tamang Heritage Trail was developed in the mid-2000s to bring tourism income to villages off the main Langtang route, and several villages run community homestay programmes. A committee assigns guests to households in rotation, sets prices and channels part of the income into a community fund for schools, trails or cultural programmes. In the Langtang Valley itself, most accommodation is in family-run lodges, which are also Tamang businesses.

sections.heading: What a homestay night is like
paras: You will usually sleep in a simple room upstairs in a stone and timber house, with a bed or mattress, blankets and perhaps a window over the terraces. The kitchen, often on the ground floor, centres on a clay stove where the family cooks and gathers. Dinner is typically dal bhat with local vegetables, potatoes and pickles, sometimes with millet or buckwheat bread; breakfast may be Tibetan bread, porridge or noodles with tea. Salt butter tea and local millet beer are offered as a welcome.

Facilities are basic. Toilets are usually shared and may be outside, hot water is limited, and electricity may come from small hydro schemes or solar panels. What you gain is time with a family: watching them cook, learning a few words of Tamang, hearing about children working in Kathmandu or abroad, and joining in the evening's songs if there is a cultural programme.

sections.heading: Food and drink in Tamang villages
paras: Tamang food is simple, filling and shaped by what grows on steep hill terraces. Dal bhat is the everyday meal, as everywhere in Nepal, but in homes you will also find dhindo, a thick porridge of millet or buckwheat flour eaten with vegetable curry or gundruk, a fermented leafy green. Potatoes are a staple at higher villages, boiled and eaten with a fiery tomato and chilli pickle, and local greens and radish appear in most meals.

Tibetan influences show in Tibetan bread, thukpa noodle soup and salt butter tea. Millet is also used to brew chhyang and the warm beer known as tongba in some areas, and stronger distilled spirits are made at home and offered at festivals. You are welcome to decline alcohol politely. In the upper Langtang Valley, yak and chauri cheese and curd are popular. Vegetarian guests will eat well, as most daily meals contain little or no meat.

sections.heading: Etiquette for visitors
paras: Tamang hosts are generous and forgiving of mistakes, but a few customs make a big difference. Your guide will help, and a smile and willingness to try go a long way.
list: Greet people with tashi delek or namaste; elders appreciate a slight bow
Remove shoes before entering a home or gompa
Do not step over the hearth or point your feet at the family shrine
Accept food and drink with your right hand or both hands
Walk clockwise around chortens, mani walls and stupas
Ask before photographing people, especially elders and religious rituals
Dress modestly; cover shoulders and knees in villages
Pay the agreed homestay price; small gifts like fruit or stationery are welcome but optional

sections.heading: How to plan a cultural trip
paras: The easiest way to experience Tamang culture is the 7-day Tamang Heritage Trail, which includes homestay nights in Gatlang and Briddim, the Tatopani hot springs and the Nagthali viewpoint at 3,165 m. It can be combined with the Langtang Valley trek for a 12–13 day trip that adds Kyanjin Gompa and the glaciers. Families with children find the homestays especially rewarding, as children often play together without needing a shared language. Time your visit for Sonam Lhosar in January or February to see the community at its most festive, or for October and November for the clearest views. Prices for our 7-day Tamang Heritage Trail start at about ₹44,000 or US$ 520 per person.

faqs.q: Who are the Tamang people of Langtang?
faqs.a: The Tamang are one of Nepal's largest ethnic groups, living mainly in the hills around Kathmandu, including Rasuwa district where Langtang lies. They speak Tamang, a Tibeto-Burman language, practise Tibetan-influenced Buddhism alongside shamanic traditions, and are known for Tamang Selo music and stone-built villages.

faqs.q: What is the Tamang Heritage Trail?
faqs.a: The Tamang Heritage Trail is a 5–7 day trek through Tamang villages west and north of Syabrubesi, including Gatlang, Tatopani, Nagthali, Thuman and Briddim. It was set up in the mid-2000s to spread tourism income to communities off the main Langtang route and features homestays and hot springs.

Yes. Homestays on the Tamang Heritage Trail are organised through community committees, and hosts are used to trekkers. Rooms are simple but clean. As anywhere, keep valuables with you and follow your guide's advice. Families with children and solo women travellers stay regularly.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay cost in Gatlang?
faqs.a: Community homestay prices are set by the village committee and typically cover a bed, dinner and breakfast. Expect roughly ₹2,000–3,000 per person per night in local terms, though prices change. On our Tamang Heritage Trail package, homestay and community fees are included.

Tamang Selo is the traditional folk music of the Tamang people: call-and-response songs about love, work and village life, sung to the rhythm of the damphu frame drum. Communities perform Selo at festivals and weddings, and homestay villages can arrange a performance for visitors.

Sonam Lhosar, the Tamang New Year, falls on the first day of the bright half of the month of Magh, usually between late January and mid-February. It is a public holiday in Nepal. Dates follow the lunar calendar and change each year; check current status before you travel.

Yes, Langtang village and the neighbouring settlements of the upper Langtang Valley are home to Tamang families with strong Tibetan Buddhist traditions. After the 2015 avalanche destroyed the old village, survivors rebuilt a new village nearby, and most lodges are run by returning families.

faqs.q: What should I bring as a gift for a Tamang host family?
faqs.a: Gifts are optional. Fruit from Kathmandu, biscuits, tea, or notebooks and pencils for children are appreciated. Avoid giving sweets directly to children or money to children in the street. Paying the agreed homestay price fairly is the most useful contribution.

faqs.q: Are the Hyolmo people of Helambu Tamang?
faqs.a: No. The Hyolmo, or Yolmo, of Helambu are a distinct Tibetan Buddhist community with their own language, closer to Sherpa and Tibetan. They share some customs with neighbouring Tamang communities, and both groups mix in the lower Helambu villages. Homestays are available in Tarkeghyang and Melamchi Gaun.
